candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns this binary to the malware class with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking (SHAP +0.0044 to +0.0102). However, the n-gram evidence is generic and does not by itself show mining behavior. No function names or locations were provided for any n-gram, so none can be tied to a specific routine. The n-grams are also short mnemonic pairs, and most of the x86-style ones (ADD POP, CMOVZ MOV, XOR CALL, AND MOV, CALL XOR, CALL ADD, MOV JZ, CMP JL, TEST JZ, XOR XOR, TEST JS, XOR SHL) have a reported frequency of 0.000000. They contribute through the model's learned thresholds, not through demonstrable prevalence in the code. The ARM-style n-grams that do have measurable frequency (sub strb 0.001253, cmn mov 0.001747, eor sub 0.000051, mvn orr 0.000047, sub umull 0.000043, sub ldrh 0.000085) are the most concrete. Of these, eor/mvn/orr/umull combine bitwise mixing with multiply-long arithmetic, which is consistent with hash or cipher inner loops of the kind used by proof-of-work miners. The x86-style XOR XOR and XOR SHL patterns are likewise consistent with hash-style mixing. The presence of both x86-style (uppercase) and ARM-style (lowercase) mnemonics in the top features is unusual and could reflect multi-architecture content or feature-extraction artifacts. Because of this, and because the same instruction patterns also occur in benign checksum, compression, and crypto code, the evidence supports a suspicious, malware-leaning verdict but does not confirm cryptojacking specifically.
